newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - EMI to return cash, restructure in U.S.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EMI to return cash, restructure in U.S.

text.p: British music company EMI Group Plc plans to return around 500 million pounds ($820 million) to shareholders and is restructuring its north American operations, the company said on Tuesday.

EMI, one of the six companies that dominate the global music industry, took a provision of 117.2 million pounds in its last financial year to cover costs as it slices out a layer of management in the United States.
The company, whose artists range from 1960s idols The Beatles to the flavour of the moment Spice Girls, forecast only modest progress this year in the face of a strong pound and subdued industry.
EMI shares fell 47p, or more than 3.8 percent, to 1,174p as the market decided the bad news overshadowed the good in the company's statement.
"The size of the restructuring cost and the flatness of the market are two negatives outweighing the positive impact of the capital return," said Jason Crisp of brokerage SocGen.

Pre-tax profit, excluding exceptional items, rose 3.6 percent to 380.5 million pounds in the year to end-March. Pre-tax profit totalled 283.9 million once exceptional items were included and the company increased its dividend 11 percent to 30 pence per share.
Chairman Sir Colin Southgate told Reuters the currency factor was likely to wipe some 30 million pounds off profits this year, similar to its impact last year.
The global music market is worth about $40 billion annually but its rate of growth has dropped back well into single figures after several years of increases in excess of 10 percent.
Southgate said he expected growth to return to between seven and eight percent but "not this year". He said growth was likely to be under five percent in this year.
EMI, which is celebrating its centenary this year, hopes to present its proposals to return capital to shareholders at its annual meeting on July 18 and implement them shortly afterwards.
It plans to return up to 10 percent of its market value -- a total of around 500 million pounds.

It gave no details of the method it plans to employ. Analysts said EMI was probably waiting for the budget which Britain's new Labour government will present in the next few weeks before finalising its plans.

EMI has long struggled for market share in the key north American market, where it lags in fifth place behind rivals Warner, Sony, PolyGram and Bertelsmann. Outside north America it is number two behind PolyGram.
The north American restructuring is designed to cut costs, improve links with other parts of the group and begin a process of management renewal.

Ken Berry, who heads EMI Music International and the company's Virgin Records unit, has been appointed worldwide president of EMI Recorded Music, adding control of the EMI Capitol label to his responsibilities.
EMI Capitol's New York head office is to close as part of a shake-up which is expected to cut operating costs by 35-40 million pounds annually, just under half of that amount coming this year.
Southgate said he intends to retire in July 2000, and added that the U.S. move was part of a three-year plan.
EMI is the only music major not part of a larger group and has long been seen as a takeover target. The decline in its share price in recent months is partly due to the failure of a bidder to emerge.
Southgate flatly denied rumours that EMI had held merger talks with Canadian drinks and entertainment group Seagram, which operates the MCA music business.($ = 0.610 British Pounds)
